The process of a Constitutional Amendment is explicitly laid out. In general, an amendment has to be authored and then put before each state for ratification. Three-fourths of the states (currently 38 of 50) have to agree and ratify it. At that point, it essentially becomes an amendment as the rest of the process is formality.

There are two problems trying to amend the Constitution:

  1. The government is not in the practice of quickly or easily reversing itself. This is by design so that we can't easily and permanently legislate on a whim or emotional outburst. Reversals like this make for a compromised set of rights and decrease faith in the government. The 18th and 21st amendments are a testament to that (Prohibition and its repeal). The Constitution and its amendments have since been largely seen as a place where rights are given, not taken away.

  2. Once enough states realize that they can indeed group together under some legal banner and pass an amendment, they will realize that they can call a Constitutional Convention far more easily, only requiring a 2/3rds vote/agreement of the states (34 currently). At this point, the barn doors are open, so to speak, for additional legislation and changes to the government. Any proposed changes would still need to have a 3/4ths vote of the states (38 again) to ratify any changes. The danger here is that the states will have finally realized that they can indeed band together to make these changes. Given the track record of Congress voting how they want instead of as representatives of the people, this isn't necessarily a good thing.
